claims.text: A metadynamics-based free-energy sampling approach can determine melting temperature, fusion enthalpy and entropy, melting volume change, and liquid-phase thermodynamic properties for single-phase high-entropy alloys.
The proposed approach can determine these properties efficiently.
Predictions from the approach will be within approximately 5% of experimental calorimetric measurements.
Equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi is an example of the single-phase HEAs to which the proposed method is intended to apply.
The simulated initial state is crystalline and near its melting point.
A tailored metadynamics protocol biases and samples the free-energy landscape across the solid-liquid transition.
High temperatures, sufficient thermal fluctuations, and adequate barrier sampling are required to sample the melting transition.
The relevant free-energy landscape reflects configurational and thermal entropy contributions.
Evolution of this free-energy landscape mediates the transition from an ordered crystal to a disordered liquid.
Metadynamics bias potentials overcome the high free-energy barriers that hinder sampling of rare melting events.
Metadynamics can directly map free-energy wells corresponding to the solid and liquid phases.
The melting temperature can be located from the crossing of solid and liquid free-energy curves.
Fusion enthalpy and entropy can be extracted from free-energy differences and slopes at the transition.
The volume change at melting can be quantified from the metadynamics simulation and validated using lattice-parameter measurements and experimental dilatometry.
Liquid-phase heat capacity and other thermodynamic properties can be obtained from free-energy curvature.
Traditional calorimetry requires extensive experimental sampling, while empirical computational models fail to capture the multicomponent energy landscape of HEAs fully.
Significant short-range order, second-phase precipitation, or an extremely rugged free-energy landscape may reduce accuracy by impeding convergence.
The method's applicability is primarily limited to idealized single-phase HEAs.
Accuracy may vary with alloy composition, simulation parameters, convergence, and local chemical inhomogeneity.
A deviation greater than 10% from experiment in melting temperature, fusion enthalpy or entropy, or melting volume change would falsify the proposed approach.
